v1.0 (spec/machine-spec.md §4.1, §4.5, §4.13) — one tile; accesses from any chunk; the areas' internals are out of scope
A. The SRAM read queue: fixed priority, steering, a second-part register (§4.5, §4.1's area interface)

An area serves its head every cycle it holds one, so after any cycle it holds at most
depth − 1 requests: 7 at the depth of 8 [meas: MemTest] (§4.1).
A read refused by a full area is not taken:
the client holds it; in a group run that is drift
(fig 6.2). A span's part 1 is sent the next cycle,
ahead of every client (none is taken that cycle):
in a group run that costs a cycle and sets drift.

area access; it reads 0, in order.

C. Contention, cycle by cycle: a gather value, the address generator (a group run), the read port, and a write tie
t: the gather value wins; area 2 is ready, so it is taken.
t+1: the address generator is granted, but area 5 is full:
not taken, and the read port gets nothing (no bypass).
Drift is set at the end of t+1 (a group run, fig 6.2).
t+2: area 5 has room; the request is taken.
t+3: the read port is granted. Area 1 also gets a write
from the write engine: both push, the write first.

• No request storage in the SRAM read queue beyond the part 1 register: a refused request waits in its client, and with no bypass nobody else is served that cycle. Fixed priority still keeps the address
generator unstarved in a digit all-to-all, where only a waiting read port competes with it (§4.5). A full token FIFO (figure 7.3) also refuses, with the same effect (§4.1).

• The write side never waits for the reads: on a tie the write goes in first (writes can't wait; reads can). A write that finds its area full stalls the write engine; a sustained overload overflows its
4-entry input FIFO, condition 2 (figure 2.4), since the traffic director never stalls.

• Alignment: none required (§4.1). A read or write may start at any chunk; one that crosses a row boundary is two area accesses, row and row + 1 (the next area after an area's last row): a read's part 1

comes from the part 1 register the next cycle, a write's second push from the write engine. Cost: one extra area access. In a group run a spanning read also costs a cycle and sets drift (§4.1, figure 2.4
bit 0): whether a read spans depends on each tile's own buffer addresses, so tiles would fall out of lockstep. Group runs use row-aligned elements; stream runs have no timetable and are unaffected.
• Out of range on a smaller device: a read (or a span's out-of-range part) is taken with no area access, its chunks read 0; a write is dropped. Neither sets a condition.
junction (crossings without a dot don't connect)
The SRAM read queue grants the highest-priority valid reader, steers its request to the area chunk[19:17], and takes it if that area has room; a read
that crosses a row boundary sends its second row the next cycle. Each area has one request queue for reads and writes in arrival order, two pushes a
cycle with the write first, and serves one 128-bit row a cycle; writes use per-chunk enables, and reads return the row with its tag and part.
